Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Jeannie Longo-Ciprelli would be remembered as the greatest female cyclist of her generation even if she had never been an Olympic champion. Longo-Ciprelli: Fourth time lucky in Atlanta in 1996. For much of her career, the Olympic gold was the one honor to elude the French rider. Misfortune, it seemed, was to be her fate every four years, regardless of how many world championships she won in between. In 1984 the first women's Olympic road race coincided with Longo-Ciprelli's rise to dominance in the sport. Well-placed going into the final lap, she appeared set to challenge in the sprint, only to be knocked off in a collision. By 1988, Longo-Ciprelli was a three-time road race world champion, as well as a double winner of the women's Tour de France, and the clear favorite for gold in Seoul. But a broken hip a month before the Games derailed her preparations. Although she recovered enough to ride the road race, she could manage just 21st place. Tactical error More disappointment followed in Barcelona in 1992 as Longo-Ciprelli paid the price for a tactical error. With three kilometers to go, she raced away from the peloton and crossed the line in celebration. But she had failed to realize that Kathy Watt, an unheralded Australian, had slipped away from the lead group apparently unnoticed with a lap to go, and finished 20 seconds further in front. Four years later, in Atlanta, Longo-Ciprelli, finally cracked her Olympic jinx. At 37, Longo-Ciprelli was no longer the dominant presence she had once been, but she still possessed the ability to raise her performance for the biggest races, as she had proven by winning her fourth road race world title in 1995. Her preparations were typically unorthodox -- while her rivals were acclimatizing to the Atlanta heat, Longo-Ciprelli trained alone in the mountains of Colorado, arriving just two days before the race. The race itself was run in a sudden downpour, which sent many riders crashing and skidding and had the rest struggling to stay on their bikes. Unruffled, Longo-Ciprelli broke clear with two other riders and then launched her gold-winning solo attack 11 kilometers from the finish. Longo-Ciprelli was back for her fifth and final Olympics in Sydney in 2000 at the age of 41, this time claiming bronze in the time trial -- and event in which she had also won silver in 1996. One prize, however, remained stubbornly out of reach: an Olympic gold medal.

# Longo-Ciprelli: Fourth time lucky in Atlanta in 1996

**By CNN Sport**

Jeannie Longo-Ciprelli arrived in Atlanta as one of cycling’s most decorated champions, yet the prize she wanted most had repeatedly eluded her.

The Frenchwoman had already amassed a remarkable collection of world titles on the road and track. She won five road-race world championships between 1985 and 1995 and would eventually claim four world time-trial crowns, part of a career total of 13 senior world titles.

The Olympics, however, had brought only frustration.

Longo finished sixth when women’s road cycling made its Olympic debut in Los Angeles in 1984. Four years later in Seoul she again missed the medals, and at Barcelona in 1992 she had to settle for silver behind Australian Kathy Watt.

By 1996, Longo was 37 and competing at her fourth Games. Her methods remained characteristically unconventional: she prepared largely outside the French federation system, working closely with her husband and coach, Patrice Ciprelli. Their approach emphasized altitude work, meticulous physiological preparation and a fiercely individual training program.

In the Atlanta road race, Longo refused to wait for a mass finish. She launched the decisive attack late in the 104-kilometer contest, using the closing climbs to break up the leading group. Italy’s Imelda Chiappa stayed close, but Longo held her off in the final run to the line.

After more than 2½ hours of racing, she crossed the finish two seconds clear of Chiappa. Canada’s Clara Hughes took bronze.

At last, on her fourth attempt, Longo-Ciprelli was Olympic champion.

She added a silver medal in Atlanta’s inaugural women’s individual time trial, behind Russia’s Zulfiya Zabirova, confirming that age had done little to blunt her range or endurance.

Four years later in Sydney, at 41, Longo-Ciprelli returned to the Olympic podium with bronze in the time trial. It was her fourth and final Olympic medal, though not her final Games: she later competed in Athens in 2004 and Beijing in 2008.

Her longevity was extraordinary, but Atlanta remained the defining Olympic moment — the day a multiple world champion finally turned years of disappointment into gold.
